newsitem.title: USA: Cohen stresses painful choices to Congress.
newsitem.headline: Cohen stresses painful choices to Congress.

text.p: Defense Secretary William Cohen on Thursday presented Congress with a new U.S. security plan for minimal troop reductions and weaponary, stressing instead a need for cuts in infrastructure such as expensive military bases.

"He (Cohen) framed it in terms of the tough choices that are necessary in order to come up with the funding and to suppoort the strategy we have for the next 15 or 20 years," Defense Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters.
Bacon spoke to reporters after Cohen presented the results of the Pentagon's quadrennial defense review to leaders of key Congressional committees at a breakfast in his Pentagon office.

Cohen was silent at a breakfast photo session but defense officials have said the so-called "QDR," due to be made public on Monday, calls for new domestic base closings and shrinking costly jet fighter programs. But it would cut only some 60,000 troops from the 1.4 million-member military.

"It (the QDR) has determined as the secretary said that we are not able right now to make significant changes in our forces structure or the number of people that we have in the military" in order to remain engaged in world affairs, Bacon told reporters.

The report, which has already drawn criticism from Congress for its call for politically-explosive base closings, and from analysts because it is not sweeping enough, seeks a continued high overseas military presence and arms modernization into the 21st century.

Bright flowers centered each of three tables in Cohen's office where he fed breakfast and charts full of figures to about 30 senior lawmakers and staffers from four key security and appropriations committees of the House and Senate.
Cohen also outlined the plan at a Pentagon lunch for former Defense Secretaries William Perry, Harold Brown, Dick Cheney, Elliot Richardson and Donald Rumsfeld.

Cohen, who retired earlier this year as a Republican senator from Maine, was flanked at his breakfast table by Chairmen Floyd Spence, a South Carolina Republican, of the House National Security Committee, and Ted Stevens, an Alaska Republican, of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
Senior Republican and Democratic lawmakers and staff directors from the Senate Armed Services Committee and House Appropriations Committees also attended.

Cohen has described the QDR results as a compromise to face the realities of growing demands on the military such as fighting wars, keeping the peace and performing humanitarian duties along with saving money to spend on needed arms modernization for the 21st century.

Some defense analysts have said more sweeping changes are needed, such as completely realigning Army divisions. And some have said the expectation of $250 billion defense budgets for the long term is unrealistic because of future demands from other federal programs.

Cohen emphasized in recent weeks that the death of the Soviet Union had not ended international threats to U.S. security and that more domestic military bases must be shut to save money for new high-tech weapons.

He made clear that the United States would retain its current strategy of being prepared to fight two major regional conflicts at once and will keep 100,000 troops in Europe and another 100,000 in the western Pacific.

Defense officials earlier confirmed a Washington Post report that Cohen planned to seek a cut of about 60,000 active duty military personnel, 70,000 military reservists and some 80,000 civilian Defense Department personnel.

They said Cohen had decided to reduce by more than 300 -- but not cancel -- the planned purchase of Air Force F-22 and Navy FA-18E/F fighter jets in programs under development by Lockheed Martin Corp and McDonnell Douglas Corp
